questions.subtopic: 2B2 Business impact analysis (BIA). Tolerable data loss
questions.question: The sales director of an events ticketing firm tells the risk practitioner that losing more than one hour of ticket sales records would be unacceptable. How should the practitioner BEST record this in the BIA?

options.A: A one-hour recovery point objective for ticket sales
options.B: A one-hour recovery time objective for ticket sales
options.C: A one-year retention period for sales backups
options.D: A one-hour maximum tolerable outage for ticket sales

questions.key_concept: A limit on tolerable data loss is recorded as the RPO; time to recover is the RTO, and the longest tolerable disruption is the MTO.
questions.pre_read: Notice exactly what the director says would be unacceptable.
questions.correct_explanation: The director has limited lost data, not downtime: no more than one hour of sales records may be lost. That is a recovery point objective, so the BIA records a one-hour RPO for sales records, and IT designs backup or replication to meet it. A one-hour RTO is the runner-up: it limits how long recovery takes, yet a fast restore can still bring back data that is a day old.

wrong_explanations.B: An RTO limits how long recovery may take; however, the director limited lost data, and a fast restore can still bring back data that is a day old.
wrong_explanations.C: A retention period sets how long backup copies are kept; it does not limit how many hours of recent sales records can be lost.
wrong_explanations.D: The MTO is the longest disruption the business can tolerate; the director limited lost records, not how long ticket sales can stop.

tips: Eliminate: C confuses how long backups are kept with how much data can be lost, and D turns a data-loss limit into an outage limit.
Final two: A beats B because the director's limit is on lost data, which is the RPO; an RTO limits recovery time and can still bring back day-old data.
Exam cue: RPO is how much data you can lose, which sets copy frequency; RTO is how long you can wait. Set and check each separately.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Business impact analysis (BIA). Recovery time beyond the outage limit
questions.question: A distributor's BIA sets a 24-hour maximum tolerable outage for order processing, but IT's tested recovery plan restores the order system in 36 hours. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Extend the order process's MTO to 36 hours in the BIA
options.B: Report the gap to the owner of order processing
options.C: Ask the recovery control owner to buy a faster service
options.D: Record the owner's RTO as 36 hours to match IT's capability

questions.key_concept: An RTO must fit inside the maximum tolerable outage; when recovery cannot meet it, the process owner decides how to close the gap.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the business can tolerate with what IT can deliver before choosing a step.
questions.correct_explanation: The business can tolerate 24 hours without order processing, but tested recovery takes 36, so a real outage would cause unacceptable harm. Closing the gap costs money, so the order-processing owner, whose tolerance the BIA records, weighs faster recovery against the impact. Buying a faster service is the runner-up: it may be the answer, but committing spend before the owner weighs the options takes the owner's decision.

wrong_explanations.A: The MTO reflects how long the business can survive the outage; stretching it to match IT's recovery time hides the harm instead of reducing it.
wrong_explanations.C: A faster service may close the gap; however, the owner should weigh its cost against the BIA impact before anyone commits the spend.
wrong_explanations.D: Recovery objectives come from business tolerance, not from what IT can deliver today; recording 36 hours as the owner's RTO accepts a gap the business never agreed to.

tips: Eliminate: A bends the business tolerance to fit IT, and D sets the RTO from IT's capability instead of the BIA.
Final two: B beats C because the owner whose tolerance is breached decides how to close the gap; buying a service first spends money the owner has not weighed.
Exam cue: the RTO must sit inside the MTO. When recovery cannot meet it, take the gap to the business owner rather than changing the numbers or buying a fix.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Business impact analysis (BIA). Missing AI service dependency
questions.question: A city's permit office relies on a vendor's AI service to read permit applications, but its BIA lists only the permit database as a dependency. What is the GREATEST risk of leaving the BIA unchanged?

options.A: The vendor's own continuity plan would go unreviewed
options.B: The AI service's failure rate would go unmeasured
options.C: Recovery plans would omit a resource the process needs
options.D: Drift in the AI model's accuracy would go unnoticed

questions.key_concept: A BIA that omits a dependency leaves that resource out of recovery planning.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the BIA is missing.
questions.correct_explanation: A BIA tells recovery planning which resources each critical process needs and how soon. With the AI service missing, no one sets a recovery requirement for it, so continuity plans and the vendor contract may not restore it before applications back up. An unreviewed vendor plan is the runner-up: it matters, but the city can only judge that plan against a requirement the BIA has not yet set.

wrong_explanations.A: Reviewing the vendor's plan matters; however, it can only be judged against a recovery requirement that the BIA has not yet set for the service.
wrong_explanations.B: A failure rate is a likelihood input for the risk assessment; a BIA assumes the disruption happens and measures its impact over time.
wrong_explanations.D: Watching model accuracy is AI performance monitoring; a BIA records dependencies and the impact of losing them, not model drift.

tips: Eliminate: B asks a BIA for likelihood, and D expects it to monitor model accuracy; neither is what a BIA does.
Final two: C beats A because the BIA sets the recovery requirement first; a vendor's plan is only judged against it.
Exam cue: when a process gains a new dependency, especially an AI or cloud service, the BIA must list it, or recovery planning will miss it.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Business impact analysis (BIA). Objective for the alternate site
questions.question: When the risk practitioner records a bank's BIA results, which objective is MOST appropriate for stating how much of normal payment volume branch payments must handle at the alternate site?

options.A: The recovery time objective
options.B: The recovery point objective
options.C: The acceptable interruption window
options.D: The service delivery objective

questions.key_concept: The service delivery objective sets the level of service needed during alternate processing; RTO and AIW are time limits, and RPO limits data loss.
questions.pre_read: Notice exactly what the objective must state.
questions.correct_explanation: The service delivery objective (SDO) is the level of service the business needs while it runs in alternate mode, until normal operation is restored. Stating the share of payment volume the alternate site must handle sets that level and drives the site's capacity. The RTO is the runner-up: it sets how soon payments must be running again, not how much service they must deliver once they are.

wrong_explanations.A: The RTO sets how soon payments must be running again after a disruption; however, it says nothing about how much volume the alternate site must then handle.
wrong_explanations.B: The RPO sets how much data loss is tolerable, which drives backup frequency; it does not set a level of service during alternate processing.
wrong_explanations.C: The AIW is the longest a system can be unavailable before objectives suffer; it is a time limit, not the service level required at the alternate site.

tips: Eliminate: B limits data loss, and C limits how long a system can be down; neither sets a service level.
Final two: D beats A because the bank must state how much service runs in alternate mode; the RTO only sets how soon recovery happens.
Exam cue: RTO, MTO and AIW say how soon; RPO says how much data; SDO says how much service while running in alternate mode.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Risk register. Entries for a retired system
questions.question: A bus operator has retired its old mobile ticketing app, and the IT manager asks the risk analyst to delete the app's four entries from the risk register. What is the analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Delete the entries once the IT owner confirms retirement
options.B: Close the entries with the risk owners' approval
options.C: Keep the entries open until the register review
options.D: Move the entries to the IT team's operational issue log

questions.key_concept: Register entries are closed, not deleted, with a recorded reason and the risk owner's approval, so the history stays available.
questions.pre_read: Think about what the register's history is for before deciding what happens to the entries.
questions.correct_explanation: Retiring the app may remove the risk, but the register keeps the record: the entries are closed with the reason, such as retirement and data disposal, and the risk owners' approval. That history supports trend analysis, audits and later questions about the app's data. Deleting them once IT confirms retirement is the runner-up: it reflects the change, but erases the record and lets IT make a closure decision that belongs to the owners.

wrong_explanations.A: IT's confirmation is useful evidence; however, deleting erases the risk history, and closing an entry is the risk owner's decision, not IT's.
wrong_explanations.C: Leaving entries open for a system that no longer exists overstates the risk profile until the review, and still needs the owners' decision later.
wrong_explanations.D: An operational issue log is not where enterprise risk is tracked; moving the entries hides their history from risk owners and the risk profile.

tips: Eliminate: C keeps a retired system's risks open as if nothing changed, and D moves risk records out of the register into an IT log.
Final two: B beats A because entries are closed with a reason and the owner's approval, keeping the history; deleting them erases it and lets IT decide.
Exam cue: register entries close on evidence and with the risk owner's approval; they are not simply deleted.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Risk register. Signs of a current register
questions.question: Which of the following BEST shows that an airport operator's IT risk register is being kept current?

options.A: Ratings revised after incidents and failed tests
options.B: Entry reviews held at the scheduled risk workshop
options.C: Entries closed on the day treatment plans are approved
options.D: A total number of entries that keeps growing

questions.key_concept: A current register changes when evidence changes: incidents, control test results, audit findings and business changes trigger updates between scheduled reviews.
questions.pre_read: Ask what should make a register entry change, and which option shows that happening.
questions.correct_explanation: A register is current when its ratings follow the evidence: an incident, near miss or failed control test changes likelihood or control effectiveness, so the affected entries are revised promptly. Ratings revised after such events show that link working. The scheduled workshop is the runner-up: scheduled reviews matter, but on their own they leave the register months behind events.

wrong_explanations.B: Scheduled reviews are part of maintenance; however, a register reviewed only at set dates can be months behind the incidents and test failures that change risk.
wrong_explanations.C: An approved plan reduces nothing until it is implemented and working; closing entries on approval makes the register look better than reality.
wrong_explanations.D: A growing count shows that entries are being added, not that existing ratings reflect today's incidents and control results.

tips: Eliminate: C closes entries on approved plans, which reduce nothing yet, and D counts entries instead of checking whether ratings are up to date.
Final two: A beats B because event-driven updates keep ratings current between reviews; a scheduled review alone can leave them months out of date.
Exam cue: a current register is evidence-driven. Look for ratings that move when incidents, tests and changes happen, not just on a calendar.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Risk analysis methodologies. Cost of the top-ranked risks
questions.question: After a qualitative first ranking of 70 IT risk scenarios, a manufacturer's board asks what the top five could cost. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Convert the 70 ratings to costs using scale midpoints
options.B: Explain that the top five ratings cannot show cost
options.C: Estimate loss ranges for the top five scenarios
options.D: Redo the 70 scenarios with quantitative loss models

questions.key_concept: Methods combine: screen many risks qualitatively, then quantify the few top risks where loss data supports a credible figure.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the board is asking for, and about which risks.
questions.correct_explanation: The board's question is about cost, which qualitative levels cannot answer, but it concerns only the top five. Quantifying those five, from loss data and expert ranges with the uncertainty stated, gives the board money figures where they matter. Redoing all 70 quantitatively is the runner-up: it would also produce costs, but at heavy effort, and for most scenarios thin data would make the figures falsely precise.

wrong_explanations.A: Scale midpoints turn ordinal levels into numbers that look exact but were never estimated, giving the board false precision across the whole list.
wrong_explanations.B: The ratings cannot show cost as they stand; however, the board's question can be answered by quantifying the few risks it is asking about.
wrong_explanations.D: Quantitative models need good data and effort; spending them on 70 scenarios, most with thin data, is disproportionate when the board asked about five.

tips: Eliminate: A turns ordinal levels into invented costs, and B declines a question that analysis can answer.
Final two: C beats D because quantitative effort goes only where the board's decision needs it; redoing all 70 adds effort and false precision.
Exam cue: methods combine. Screen many risks qualitatively, then quantify the top few where data supports a credible figure.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Risk analysis methodologies. Simulated loss against tolerance
questions.question: A marketplace's Monte Carlo fraud run gives yearly losses averaging $300,000, with a 5% chance of exceeding $1,200,000. The board's limit is a 5% chance of exceeding $1,000,000; what is the risk analyst's BEST conclusion?

options.A: Not comparable until rated high, medium or low
options.B: Within tolerance, judged on the $300,000 mean
options.C: Undecidable until the model gives one figure
options.D: Beyond tolerance, judged on the $1,200,000 figure

questions.key_concept: Compare a simulated loss distribution with tolerance as written; a limit on the chance of a large loss is tested on the tail.
questions.pre_read: Notice what each figure from the simulation measures.
questions.correct_explanation: The board's tolerance is a probability: at most a 5% chance of losing over $1,000,000 in a year. The simulation gives a 5% chance of losing more than $1,200,000, so the chance of exceeding $1,000,000 is above 5%: the scenario is beyond tolerance. Judging on the $300,000 mean is the runner-up: it is the expected loss, but a limit on rare large losses is tested against the distribution's tail, not its average.

wrong_explanations.A: Rating the result high, medium or low throws away the probabilities the board's tolerance is written in; the simulation can be compared with it directly.
wrong_explanations.B: The mean is the expected yearly loss; however, the board set its tolerance on the chance of a large loss, which the mean does not show.
wrong_explanations.C: A Monte Carlo result is a distribution by design; asking for a single figure discards the tail information the tolerance needs.

tips: Eliminate: A and C refuse to compare, yet the simulation's probabilities match the way the tolerance is written.
Final two: D beats B because the tolerance limits the chance of a large loss; the mean says nothing about the tail.
Exam cue: compare a simulated loss distribution with a limit in the form the limit is written; a probability limit is tested on the tail, not the average.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Risk analysis methodologies. Equal scores on a matrix
questions.question: On a bank's risk matrix, card skimming (40 small losses a year) and a week-long banking outage (once in 20 years) both score 10. How should the risk analyst BEST present them to the committee?

options.A: With likelihood and impact shown for each scenario
options.B: As equal-priority scenarios with the same score
options.C: With the outage ranked higher for its larger impact
options.D: With each score converted to a loss figure in dollars

questions.key_concept: A combined matrix score shows order, not the shape of a risk; equal scores can hide very different likelihood and impact that need different responses.
questions.pre_read: Notice how each scenario reaches its score of 10.
questions.correct_explanation: The equal scores hide two different risks: about 40 small skimming losses a year call for mitigating controls, while a severe outage expected once in 20 years may call for continuity planning or transfer. Showing likelihood and impact separately lets the committee see that difference. Treating them as equal priorities is the runner-up: the matrix does rank them equally, but the score is ordinal and the decision needs the shape behind it.

wrong_explanations.B: The shared score is a fair ranking signal; however, it hides whether the risk comes from frequency or severity, which the committee needs to choose responses.
wrong_explanations.C: Ranking on impact alone drops likelihood, so the frequent skimming losses would be undervalued however often they occur.
wrong_explanations.D: Converting ordinal matrix scores into money produces precise-looking numbers the data does not support, adding false precision instead of clarity.

tips: Eliminate: C ranks on one dimension only, and D turns ordinal scores into invented money figures.
Final two: A beats B because equal scores can hide opposite risk profiles; showing both dimensions gives the committee what it needs to choose different responses.
Exam cue: matrix scores are ordinal. When the decision depends on how a risk arises, report likelihood and impact, not just the combined score.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Risk analysis methodologies. Expected loss from outage history
questions.question: Each outage of a parcel firm's sorting system costs about $120,000, and the system has failed three times in the past six years. What is the risk analyst's BEST estimate of the annualized loss expectancy?

options.A: About $20,000 a year
options.B: About $40,000 a year
options.C: About $60,000 a year
options.D: About $360,000 a year

questions.key_concept: ALE equals single loss expectancy times annual rate of occurrence; three events in six years is an ARO of 0.5.
questions.pre_read: Identify each part of the ALE formula from the stem before choosing a figure.
questions.correct_explanation: The SLE is $120,000, the cost of one outage. Three outages in six years is an ARO of 0.5, half an outage a year, so the ALE is $120,000 times 0.5, about $60,000 a year. The $20,000 figure is the runner-up: it treats the six-year window as one outage every six years, missing that three occurred. An ALE is only as good as this history, so its source is stated.

wrong_explanations.A: This treats the rate as one outage every six years; three outages in six years is an ARO of 0.5, not about 0.17.
wrong_explanations.B: This divides the cost by the number of outages; ALE multiplies the cost of one outage by how many occur each year.
wrong_explanations.D: This is the total loss over all six years, not the expected loss in one year.

tips: Eliminate: B divides the cost by the number of outages, and D gives the six-year total instead of a yearly figure.
Final two: C beats A because three outages in six years is an ARO of 0.5; A uses one outage in six years.
Exam cue: convert history to an annual rate first (events divided by years), then multiply the single loss by that rate.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286A Rev. 1 Section 2.2.4 (Determining Potential Impact: single loss expectancy and annualized loss expectancy)

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Inherent and residual risk. Large gap from one control
questions.question: An online game publisher's account takeover scenario has very high inherent risk but low current risk, almost entirely because of one bot-detection control. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend as MOST important?

options.A: Lowering the inherent rating to match current risk
options.B: Regular testing of the bot-detection control
options.C: A KRI on the volume of account takeover attempts
options.D: Raising current risk to reflect the reliance

questions.key_concept: A wide gap between inherent and current risk marks reliance on a key control, so that control's continued effectiveness needs regular evidence.
questions.pre_read: Notice where the low current rating comes from.
questions.correct_explanation: Low current risk here rests almost entirely on one control, so if bot detection weakens, the risk jumps back toward its very high inherent level. Regular testing, backed by key control indicators, shows whether the control still works and keeps the current rating honest. A KRI on attempt volume is the runner-up: it tracks the threat, but steady or rising attempts say nothing about whether the control is still stopping them.

wrong_explanations.A: Inherent risk ignores all management action, controls included, so it does not fall because a control works; changing it would hide how much the scenario depends on that control.
wrong_explanations.C: Attempt volume is a useful threat signal; however, it cannot show whether the single control holding the risk down is still working.
wrong_explanations.D: Reliance on one control is a concentration to watch, not a reason to re-rate; current risk reflects how well the control works today, which only testing shows.

tips: Eliminate: A lowers inherent risk because of a control, which inherent risk does not count, and D re-rates the risk for reliance instead of checking whether the control still works.
Final two: B beats C because the current rating is only as good as the control behind it; attempt volume tracks the threat, not the control.
Exam cue: high inherent and low current risk means a key control. Make sure there is regular evidence that it keeps working.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Inherent and residual risk. Paper for a tolerance breach
questions.question: Failed access reviews push a pension fund's member-data scenario beyond the executive committee's tolerance; the risk owner asks the committee to accept it for a quarter. What MOST belongs in the risk practitioner's committee paper?

options.A: The owner's case for exceeding the tolerance
options.B: The cost of an automated access review tool
options.C: The count of access reviews failed this year
options.D: Current risk set against the breached tolerance

questions.key_concept: A request to accept a tolerance breach goes to whoever set the limit, with the current risk measured against that limit.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the committee is being asked to decide.
questions.correct_explanation: The committee is asked to accept a risk above a limit it set, so the paper must show how far current risk now sits beyond that tolerance and what that means for the fund. The committee can then weigh the owner's request on the facts. The owner's case is the runner-up: the committee should hear it, but without current risk set against the tolerance it cannot judge what it is being asked to accept.

wrong_explanations.A: The owner's reasons belong in the paper; however, they cannot show the committee how far beyond its own limit the risk now sits.
wrong_explanations.B: A tool's cost informs treatment options; it does not tell the committee how much risk it is being asked to accept for the quarter.
wrong_explanations.C: The failed reviews are the cause; a count of them does not translate into exposure measured against the tolerance.

tips: Eliminate: B prices one treatment and C counts the cause; neither shows the exposure the committee is asked to accept.
Final two: D beats A because acceptance beyond tolerance turns on how far the risk exceeds the limit; the owner's case cannot show that.
Exam cue: when the level that set a limit is asked to accept a breach, lead with the current risk measured against that limit.

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Risk events. Loss threshold in event data
questions.question: A credit union's operational loss database records only IT events that caused a loss above $10,000. Which of the following is the GREATEST weakness for the risk analyst using it to rate IT risk scenarios?

options.A: It omits near misses and losses under the threshold
options.B: It values each loss in money, not on the rating scale
options.C: It leaves out loss events suffered by peer credit unions
options.D: It keeps losses from incidents closed several years ago

questions.key_concept: Event data that records only larger realized losses understates likelihood, because near misses and small losses show how often threats get through.
questions.pre_read: Notice the rule that decides what goes into the database.
questions.correct_explanation: Near misses and small losses are the most frequent evidence of how often threats reach the credit union's assets, so a $10,000 threshold makes its scenarios look less likely than they are. Peer losses are the runner-up: they add useful outside evidence, but they are a separate source to add and adjust for local exposure, not a flaw in what the internal database captures.

wrong_explanations.B: Money values suit quantitative analysis and can be mapped to the rating scale; recording losses in money does not hide any events.
wrong_explanations.C: External events are a useful extra source, adjusted for local exposure; their absence is not a defect of an internal database that records the credit union's own history.
wrong_explanations.D: Older losses still show how often and how badly the scenario has played out; they are adjusted for changes since, not dropped.

tips: Eliminate: B confuses the unit of measure with missing data, and D treats older closed incidents as useless, though they still show frequency and impact.
Final two: A beats C because the threshold strips the internal record of its most frequent evidence, while peer data is a separate source to add, not a gap in this one.
Exam cue: when event data counts only realized or large losses, expect likelihood to be understated; near misses are evidence too.

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Risk events. Event log entries with date and loss only
questions.question: Three regional offices of a freight forwarder enter IT risk events in one shared log, but most entries give only the date and the amount lost. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Loss totals reported by each office to the risk team
options.B: A loss threshold below which offices need not log events
options.C: Central ownership of the event log by the IT team
options.D: An event record that names cause, impact and scenario

questions.key_concept: Risk event data is useful only when each record names its cause, impact and the scenario it affects, not just the date and the loss.
questions.pre_read: Look at what each entry leaves out.
questions.correct_explanation: A date and a loss amount show that something went wrong, not why or which risk it bears on. Requiring each record to name the cause, the impact and the scenario affected lets events be linked to scenarios, trended by cause and used as likelihood evidence. Office loss totals are the runner-up: they summarize the money lost, but totals still cannot show cause or tie losses to scenarios.

wrong_explanations.A: Totals summarize what was lost but carry no cause or scenario, so they cannot show which risks the events bear on.
wrong_explanations.B: A threshold drops near misses and small losses, the most frequent evidence of how often threats get through, so the log would hold less than now.
wrong_explanations.C: Moving the log to IT changes who holds it, not what each entry records; the missing details would remain.

tips: Eliminate: B drops near misses and small losses, and C moves custody of the log without changing what it records.
Final two: D beats A because each event must carry its cause and scenario to count as evidence; totals only add up the losses.
Exam cue: an event record is risk evidence only when it ties cause and impact to a scenario; dates and amounts alone are bookkeeping.

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Risk events. Payment caught by a second approver
questions.question: A publishing house's accounts payable clerk keys a $45,000 supplier payment that should have been $4,500, and the second approver catches it before release. How should the risk analyst BEST record this event?

options.A: A $40,500 loss event against the payment error scenario
options.B: A corrected error that needs no entry in risk records
options.C: A near miss against the payment error scenario
options.D: A control test result for the second approval step

questions.key_concept: An event stopped by a control before any loss is a near miss and is recorded as evidence against its risk scenario.
questions.pre_read: Check what the event cost before deciding how to record it.
questions.correct_explanation: The wrong payment was stopped by a control before any money left, so this is a near miss: no loss, but proof the error can happen and that the second approval was the last barrier. A control test result is the runner-up; the event does show the approval working, but its main value is as likelihood evidence for the scenario, and one catch is not a planned test.

wrong_explanations.A: No money was paid, so there is no loss to record; $40,500 is what the error could have cost, not a realized loss.
wrong_explanations.B: Correcting the payment closes the error, not the risk; an uncounted near miss leaves the scenario's likelihood understated.
wrong_explanations.D: A control test is planned and sampled; one catch shows the approval held this time but does not test how it runs over time.

tips: Eliminate: A counts a loss that never happened, and B treats a corrected error as closed, losing evidence about how often the error occurs.
Final two: C beats D because the event's main value is as likelihood evidence for the scenario; one catch is not a planned test of the approval.
Exam cue: stopped before harm, by a control, chance or timing, means near miss; record it against the scenario it supports.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Threat modeling and threat landscape. Attack tree result
questions.question: An attack tree for a coffee chain's gift-card platform shows six fraud paths: an admin console's multifactor sign-in blocks four, and two have no control. What is the risk practitioner's BEST use of this result?

options.A: Link the six paths to MITRE ATT&CK techniques
options.B: Analyze the two open paths with the platform owner
options.C: Ask the platform owner to add controls on the open paths
options.D: Lower the fraud scenario's likelihood rating to low

questions.key_concept: An attack tree's uncontrolled paths show where a scenario's exposure sits; they are analyzed with the owner before controls are chosen.
questions.pre_read: Notice what each branch of the tree shows.
questions.correct_explanation: The tree's value is in showing where the fraud scenario is exposed: two paths reach card fraud with nothing in the way. Analyzing their likelihood and impact with the platform owner turns the result into a rating the owner can act on. Asking the owner to add controls is the runner-up: those paths may need controls, but choosing them before the exposure is analyzed skips the step that sizes the response.

wrong_explanations.A: ATT&CK adds context on how credible each technique is, but relabeling the paths does not analyze the exposure the open paths create.
wrong_explanations.C: Controls may be needed, but picking them before the two open paths are analyzed sizes the response without knowing the risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Four blocked paths do not make fraud unlikely while two paths have no control; lowering the rating hides the open exposure.

tips: Eliminate: A relabels the paths without analyzing them, and D lowers the rating although two paths still have no control.
Final two: B beats C because the open paths are analyzed with the owner first; controls are chosen once the exposure is known.
Exam cue: an attack tree's uncontrolled paths are where the scenario's exposure sits; analyze them with the owner before choosing controls.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Threat modeling and threat landscape. Openly editable training data
questions.question: A ride-hailing company plans to retrain its fare-pricing model weekly on a public traffic dataset that any user can edit. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the pricing owner to license a paid traffic feed
options.B: Rely on the model's accuracy check to catch bad inputs
options.C: Assess the data poisoning risk with the pricing owner
options.D: Assess the prompt injection risk with the pricing owner

questions.key_concept: Training data that outsiders can edit exposes a model to data poisoning, which is assessed with the business owner before controls are chosen.
questions.pre_read: Notice who can change the data the model learns from.
questions.correct_explanation: An openly editable dataset lets anyone plant records the model will learn from, which is data poisoning. The risk should be analyzed with the business owner of pricing before anyone picks a control. Relying on the accuracy check is the runner-up: targeted poisoning can skew prices for chosen routes or times while overall accuracy looks normal, so the check may not see it.

wrong_explanations.A: A licensed feed may be the right control, but choosing it before the poisoning risk is analyzed skips the assessment the owner needs to decide.
wrong_explanations.B: An overall accuracy check can miss targeted poisoning, which shifts outputs for a small set of inputs while average accuracy stays normal.
wrong_explanations.D: Prompt injection targets models that read instructions in text; the threat this design creates is poisoned training data, so the owner would assess the wrong risk.

tips: Eliminate: A picks a control before the risk is analyzed, and D names an attack on a language model's inputs, not on the training data this model learns from.
Final two: C beats B because targeted poisoning can pass an overall accuracy check; the exposure must be analyzed before any existing check is relied on.
Exam cue: when an AI model learns from data outsiders can change, think data poisoning and assess it with the business owner first.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Vulnerability management. Flaw in a shared component
questions.question: An engineering consultancy learns from a national cyber agency alert that a file-compression component built into many commercial and in-house applications has a critical flaw. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Assess business exposure from the flaw's 10.0 Base score
options.B: Ask IT to patch servers in order of their CVSS scores
options.C: Wait for each vendor to confirm its use of the component
options.D: Find which business services rely on the component

questions.key_concept: For a new flaw in a shared component, the first step is to identify where it runs and which business services depend on it.
questions.pre_read: Check what must be known before exposure can be rated.
questions.correct_explanation: Exposure cannot be rated until the consultancy knows where the component runs and which business services depend on it, so the first step is to identify the affected assets from software inventories and component lists. Waiting for vendors is the runner-up: their notices help, but they cover only commercial products, and the in-house applications using the component have no vendor to report.

wrong_explanations.A: The Base score describes the flaw's severity, not the consultancy's exposure; until it is known where the component runs, the score cannot become a risk rating.
wrong_explanations.B: Patching by score, before the affected systems are known, may fix servers that lack the component and miss services that matter most.
wrong_explanations.C: Vendor notices cover only commercial products and may be slow; the in-house applications using the component have no vendor to confirm exposure.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a severity score as the risk rating, and B patches by score before anyone knows which systems run the component.
Final two: D beats C because vendor notices cannot cover in-house software; the firm's own inventories show where the component sits and what it supports.
Exam cue: for a newly disclosed flaw, first establish where it exists and which business services depend on it; rating and fixing follow.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Vulnerability management. Weaknesses in an approval process
questions.question: Which of the following is the BEST source for the risk practitioner to identify control weaknesses in a pharmaceutical wholesaler's supplier-payment approval process?

options.A: A review of the documented approval procedure
options.B: A self-assessment questionnaire completed by the approvers
options.C: A walkthrough of each step with the payment staff
options.D: An authenticated vulnerability scan of the payment system

questions.key_concept: Process weaknesses are best found by walking through the process with the people who perform it, not from documents or self-reports.
questions.pre_read: Notice what kind of weakness the question asks about.
questions.correct_explanation: The weaknesses asked about sit in how payments are approved: missing approvals, weak segregation of duties, steps that can be skipped. Walking through each step with the staff who perform it shows how approval actually works and where it can fail. Reviewing the documented procedure is the runner-up: it shows how approval is meant to run, but weaknesses in practice, such as a skipped check, do not appear on paper.

wrong_explanations.A: The procedure shows the intended design; it cannot show steps staff skip or approvals that happen out of order.
wrong_explanations.B: A questionnaire the approvers fill in about their own process is a useful input, but self-reported answers can miss the weaknesses the approvers work around.
wrong_explanations.D: A vulnerability scan finds technical flaws in software and configuration; it cannot see a missing approval or a step staff skip.

tips: Eliminate: D looks only at technical flaws in the software, and B relies on approvers rating their own process.
Final two: C beats A because a walkthrough shows how approval runs in practice; a documented procedure shows only how it should run.
Exam cue: for process weaknesses, prefer evidence of how the process actually runs over how it is documented or self-reported.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Risk scenario development and evaluation. Gaps after executive workshops
questions.question: A freight railway built its IT risk scenarios from business objectives in executive workshops, but IT's vulnerability data shows three critical weaknesses no scenario covers. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add three scenarios covering the weaknesses IT found
options.B: Add a bottom-up review using asset and threat data
options.C: Propose that senior management re-rank the workshop scenarios
options.D: Log the three weaknesses in IT's operational issue list

questions.key_concept: Scenario development combines top-down work from objectives with bottom-up work from assets, threats and vulnerabilities, so neither view's blind spots remain.
questions.pre_read: Look at how the scenario set was built.
questions.correct_explanation: Three critical weaknesses slipped past a purely top-down method, which suggests others did too. Adding a bottom-up review from asset, threat and vulnerability data fixes the gap in the method, so the scenario set reflects both what matters to objectives and what could actually go wrong. Adding three scenarios is the runner-up: it covers what IT happened to find, not what the method still misses.

wrong_explanations.A: Three new scenarios cover these weaknesses, but the method that missed them stays unchanged, so other gaps remain unfound.
wrong_explanations.C: Re-ranking reorders the same top-down scenarios; it cannot add risks that the workshops never identified.
wrong_explanations.D: An IT issue list treats the weaknesses as technical tasks, outside the scenarios the business rates and owns.

tips: Eliminate: C repeats the top-down method that missed the weaknesses, and D treats them as IT tasks, outside the business's risk scenarios.
Final two: B beats A because the gap is in the method; three new scenarios cover what IT found, not what a one-direction approach still misses.
Exam cue: when scenarios miss real threats, combine top-down and bottom-up; fix the method, not just the instance.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Risk scenario development and evaluation. Completing a draft scenario
questions.question: A risk analyst drafts this scenario: 'Ransomware encrypts a medical supplies distributor's warehouse management system.' Which addition would MOST improve the scenario for rating?

options.A: The ransomware groups active in the sector this year
options.B: The endpoint protection tools installed on its servers
options.C: The CVSS score of the system's most severe open flaw
options.D: The effect on hospital deliveries of a two-day shutdown

questions.key_concept: A risk scenario becomes ratable when it states the business consequence and timing, not only the event and the asset.
questions.pre_read: List which parts of a scenario the draft already has.
questions.correct_explanation: The draft names an event and an asset but not the actor, the time or the consequence, so owners cannot judge impact and would rate it very differently. Adding what a two-day shutdown would do to hospital deliveries states the business harm and its timing, which makes the scenario ratable. Naming active ransomware groups is the runner-up: it fills in the actor, but the missing time and consequence are the bigger gap for rating.

wrong_explanations.A: Naming active groups fills in the actor, which sharpens likelihood; but with no duration or business consequence, owners still cannot rate impact.
wrong_explanations.B: Installed tools are existing controls, recorded beside the scenario's rating; they do not describe what happens or what it costs.
wrong_explanations.C: A CVSS score rates one technical flaw's severity; it says nothing about the business harm the scenario would cause.

tips: Eliminate: B lists existing controls and C a flaw's severity; neither describes what the event would do to the business.
Final two: D beats A because it adds two missing elements, the time and the business consequence, that owners need to rate impact; the actor refines likelihood but leaves impact unratable.
Exam cue: a ratable scenario names actor, event, asset, time and business consequence; look for the missing piece.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Risk scenario development and evaluation. Scenarios drafted by IT
questions.question: An insurer's risk team drafted 15 risk scenarios for a new claims platform in a workshop attended only by IT staff. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Refer the scenarios to internal audit for completeness
options.B: Rate the scenarios and share them with the claims owners
options.C: Benchmark the scenarios against a vendor scenario library
options.D: Have the claims process owners confirm each scenario

questions.key_concept: Risk scenarios are validated by the business owners of the processes they affect before they are rated.
questions.pre_read: Notice who was in the room when the scenarios were drafted.
questions.correct_explanation: Scenarios must be confirmed by the people who own the business impact before they are rated; here no claims manager has seen them, so their events, impacts and existing controls are unvalidated. Rating them and sharing them with the claims owners is the runner-up: the owners do see the work, but only after ratings are built on scenarios they never confirmed.

wrong_explanations.A: Internal audit gives independent assurance on the process later; it does not replace the claims owners, who know the business impact.
wrong_explanations.B: Rating before validation builds ratings on unconfirmed scenarios; sharing them with the claims owners afterwards informs them instead of drawing on what they know.
wrong_explanations.C: A vendor library is a useful starting point for drafting, but it cannot confirm that these scenarios fit this insurer's claims business.

tips: Eliminate: A hands validation to internal audit, whose independent assurance comes later, and C compares the drafts with a generic library that cannot speak for this insurer.
Final two: D beats B because owners validate scenarios before they are rated; showing them finished ratings informs them without drawing on what they know.
Exam cue: scenarios drafted without the business are validated by the business process owners before they are rated.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Risk assessment concepts and standards. Likelihood of an adversarial threat
questions.question: A risk analyst at a city transit agency is rating how likely a hacktivist group is to deface the agency's journey-planner website. Which of the following should MOST inform the likelihood rating?

options.A: The attackers' capability, intent and choice of targets
options.B: The agency's own count of past website defacement incidents
options.C: The cost to the agency of a day of defaced journey pages
options.D: The CVSS score of the website platform's worst open flaw

questions.key_concept: The likelihood of an adversarial threat event rests on the adversary's capability, intent and targeting, not mainly on past incidents.
questions.pre_read: Identify what kind of threat source the scenario involves.
questions.correct_explanation: For an adversarial threat, likelihood rests on the adversary: whether the group can carry out the attack, whether it wants to, and whether it is choosing targets like this agency. The agency's own defacement history is the runner-up; history is the main input for accidental, structural and environmental threats, but an adversary's past absence says little about its intent now.

wrong_explanations.B: History suits non-adversarial threats; an agency never defaced before can still be chosen next by a group with the intent and capability.
wrong_explanations.C: The cost of defaced pages is impact, the other half of risk; it does not tell the analyst how likely the attack is.
wrong_explanations.D: The flaw's severity score describes the weakness, not whether this group will try to use it, and is not a likelihood rating.

tips: Eliminate: C measures impact rather than likelihood, and D rates a flaw's technical severity, not the group's chance of acting.
Final two: A beats B because adversarial likelihood turns on the actor's capability, intent and targeting; history fits accidental and natural threats better.
Exam cue: for a deliberate attacker, rate likelihood from capability, intent and targeting; for other threat sources, use history and data.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.1 (Risk Models: adversarial likelihood is based on intent, capability and targeting)

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Risk assessment concepts and standards. Missing vendor evidence
questions.question: During a payroll outsourcing risk assessment at a fitness club chain, the vendor refuses to share its control audit report; signing is due next month. What is the risk practitioner's BEST action?

options.A: Report the missing evidence and how it limits the rating
options.B: Rate the vendor's controls as effective pending evidence
options.C: Pause the assessment until the vendor shares its report
options.D: Take the vendor's verbal assurance about its controls

questions.key_concept: When an assessment cannot obtain key information, it states the constraint and its effect on confidence so the decision maker knows the gap.
questions.pre_read: Notice when the decision will be made and what is unknown.
questions.correct_explanation: The owner must decide on the contract within a month, so the assessment should go ahead with the gap stated: what could not be verified and how much that lowers confidence in the vendor's rating. The owner can then sign, require the report or look elsewhere. Pausing is the runner-up: it avoids an unsupported rating, but it leaves the owner deciding with no assessment at all.

wrong_explanations.B: Crediting controls nobody has seen evidence for overstates their effect; an unverified control earns little or no credit in the rating.
wrong_explanations.C: The vendor has already refused, so the pause may never end, and signing goes ahead next month without the assessment the owner needs.
wrong_explanations.D: A verbal assurance is not evidence that controls operate; relying on it hides the gap from the owner who must decide.

tips: Eliminate: B and D credit controls nobody has seen evidence for, which overstates their effect on the rating.
Final two: A beats C because the decision will be made next month either way; a stated limitation informs it, while a paused assessment leaves the owner nothing.
Exam cue: when information is missing, state the constraint and its effect on confidence; decision makers need the gap, not silence.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Risk assessment concepts and standards. Step after rating
questions.question: A risk analyst has rated a grocery chain's loyalty-data theft scenario as high on the agreed scales. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Recommend controls to the owner to bring the rating down
options.B: Compare the rating with the risk criteria and appetite
options.C: Report the scenario to the board as above appetite
options.D: Ask the loyalty program owner to choose a response

questions.key_concept: After analysis, risk evaluation compares the rating with agreed criteria and appetite to decide whether a response is needed.
questions.pre_read: Place the analyst's work in the assessment sequence.
questions.correct_explanation: Analysis gives a rating; evaluation then sets it against the agreed risk criteria and appetite to decide whether the risk is acceptable, needs a response and how urgently. Asking the owner to choose a response is the runner-up; the owner does decide, but until evaluation shows whether a response is needed and how urgent it is, the owner has nothing to decide on.

wrong_explanations.A: Recommending controls to the owner jumps to treatment before evaluation has shown whether the rating is beyond what the chain accepts.
wrong_explanations.C: Nothing yet shows the risk is above appetite; reporting it to the board before evaluation could misstate it and bypasses the owner.
wrong_explanations.D: The owner decides the response, but only after evaluation shows whether one is needed and how urgently.

tips: Eliminate: A recommends treatment and C reports a breach before the rating has been compared with criteria and appetite.
Final two: B beats D because evaluation comes first and informs the owner's choice; without it the owner does not know whether a response is needed.
Exam cue: identify, analyze, evaluate, then respond; when a rating is new, compare it with criteria and appetite before anyone treats it.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Business impact analysis (BIA). When a process becomes critical
questions.question: Which of the following BEST shows the risk practitioner when a social security agency's benefit payment process becomes critical during an outage?

options.A: Impact estimates at set intervals of outage time
options.B: The process's worst-case loss for one day of outage
options.C: IT's tested restore time for the payment system
options.D: The estimated likelihood of a payment system outage

questions.key_concept: A BIA shows when a process becomes critical by measuring how its impact grows over intervals of outage time.
questions.pre_read: Notice exactly what the practitioner wants to learn.
questions.correct_explanation: A BIA shows how harm grows as an outage lengthens, by asking process owners what happens after one hour, one day, one week and so on; the point where impact turns severe shows when the process becomes critical and informs its MTO. The worst-case loss for one day of outage is the runner-up; it shows size, but one figure cannot show when harm becomes intolerable.

wrong_explanations.B: A single worst-day figure gives the size of the loss but not its timing; criticality depends on when harm becomes intolerable.
wrong_explanations.C: A restore time shows what IT can deliver, not when the business can no longer cope; it is checked against the BIA, not used to set it.
wrong_explanations.D: A BIA assumes the outage happens; likelihood belongs in the risk assessment, not in judging when the process becomes critical.

tips: Eliminate: C measures IT's recovery capability rather than business harm, and D brings in likelihood, which a BIA does not estimate.
Final two: A beats B because criticality depends on how impact grows over time; a one-day worst-case loss shows size but not timing.
Exam cue: in a BIA, look for impact over time from the business; that is what sets MTO and recovery priorities.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Risk register. Owner field held by IT
questions.question: A SaaS provider's IT security team maintains its risk register and is named as risk owner on all 60 entries, including customer churn after outages. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep IT security as owner while it maintains the register
options.B: Split ownership among IT team leads by business area
options.C: Propose business owners for senior management to assign
options.D: Move ownership of the entries to the risk function

questions.key_concept: Register entries need accountable business owners, proposed by the risk function and assigned by senior management, not IT or the risk team.
questions.pre_read: Ask who carries the losses the entries describe.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk owner must be an accountable business manager with authority over the response and the losses, such as whoever answers for customer retention. The risk function proposes suitable owners and senior management assigns them. Moving ownership to the risk function is the runner-up: it takes risk away from IT, but the second line maintains the register and challenges; it cannot own the business's risks.

wrong_explanations.A: Maintaining the register is an administrative role; it gives IT security no authority over business losses such as customer churn.
wrong_explanations.B: IT team leads may own controls, but they cannot decide responses for business losses outside their authority.
wrong_explanations.D: The risk function facilitates and challenges as the second line; owning the entries would leave it deciding responses it should only advise on.

tips: Eliminate: A confuses maintaining the register with owning risk, and B gives business losses to IT leads, who own controls rather than those outcomes.
Final two: C beats D because the second line advises and maintains the register; owners come from the business, assigned by senior management.
Exam cue: a risk owner is the business manager who carries the loss and can fund the response; IT and the risk function support.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Risk register. Entry for a new AI system
questions.question: A hotel group's AI room-pricing tool went live last month with no loss history; its vendor shares only launch test results. Which of the following MOST belongs in the risk practitioner's new register entry?

options.A: An ALE estimate built from other hotel groups' losses
options.B: A stated level of uncertainty in its rating
options.C: The accuracy score from the vendor's launch testing
options.D: No rating until a quarter of live pricing data exists

questions.key_concept: A new AI risk with little data is recorded early with its uncertainty stated, so the rating is not mistaken for precise knowledge.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the entry can be built from.
questions.correct_explanation: With no loss history and only the vendor's launch test results, any rating of the new tool is a judgment with wide uncertainty. Stating that uncertainty tells the owner how much weight the rating can bear and supports an early review as production evidence arrives. The vendor's launch accuracy score is the runner-up: it is real evidence, but it measures performance in testing, not exposure in the hotel group's pricing.

wrong_explanations.A: Other groups' losses turned into one ALE figure suggest precision the data cannot support for a newly launched system.
wrong_explanations.C: Launch accuracy shows how the model did in testing, not how wrong prices would affect revenue or guests in production.
wrong_explanations.D: Leaving the entry unrated while live data builds keeps a risk the hotel group already carries out of the profile; it is recorded now, with its uncertainty stated.

tips: Eliminate: A gives a precise figure the data cannot support, and D leaves a live risk unrated while data builds.
Final two: B beats C because the rating is a judgment with wide uncertainty that must be stated; launch accuracy is test evidence, not business exposure.
Exam cue: for a new or emerging risk, record it early with stated uncertainty and an owner, and review it soon.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Risk register. Ratings that judge a plan
questions.question: City council members ask whether the treatment plans in the IT risk register will bring each risk within appetite once completed. Which register field should the risk practitioner use to BEST answer them?

options.A: The target rating each planned response is set to reach
options.B: The current rating, with the controls in place today
options.C: The inherent rating, before controls are counted
options.D: The status of each action plan against its due date

questions.key_concept: Whether a treatment plan is enough is judged on its target risk, the Glossary's future residual risk, compared with appetite.
questions.pre_read: Notice the point in time the members are asking about.
questions.correct_explanation: The members want to know where each risk will land when its plan is done, which is the target, or future residual, risk the plan is designed to reach. Comparing that rating with appetite shows whether each plan is enough. The current rating is the runner-up: it is the right figure for today's position against appetite, but it cannot show where a plan will take the risk.

wrong_explanations.B: Current risk shows today's exposure and is compared with appetite now; it does not show where a completed plan would leave each risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Inherent risk ignores all controls and responses, so it cannot show the effect of any treatment plan.
wrong_explanations.D: Action status shows progress against dates, not the level of risk the finished plan will leave.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves out every response by definition, so it cannot show a plan's effect, and D tracks progress dates rather than any risk level.
Final two: A beats B because the question is about the plans once complete; current risk answers where the risk stands today.
Exam cue: today's position against appetite is current risk; whether a plan is enough is judged on its target, or future residual, risk.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Inherent and residual risk. Review threshold and fraud losses
questions.question: An electronics retailer's fraud team reviews every refund over $5,000 each day, as logs confirm, but most refund fraud losses come from refunds under $500. How should the risk practitioner BEST assess the review?

options.A: Effective in both design and operation
options.B: Effective in operation but not in design
options.C: Effective in design but not in operation
options.D: Not ratable until its operation is tested

questions.key_concept: A control that operates as designed but does not address the scenario's cause is ineffective in design and earns little residual credit.
questions.pre_read: Judge the review's design and its operation separately.
questions.correct_explanation: The logs show the review runs as intended, so it operates effectively, but its $5,000 threshold leaves out the small refunds where most fraud losses arise, so its design does not address the scenario's cause. It should earn little credit in the residual rating. Waiting for an operating test is the runner-up: a test adds assurance on operation, but no test result can fix a design that misses the losses.

wrong_explanations.A: The review runs daily, but it looks only at refunds over $5,000 while most fraud losses come from refunds under $500.
wrong_explanations.C: The logs show the review is performed each day; its weakness is what it was designed to look at, not how it runs.
wrong_explanations.D: Operating evidence already exists in the logs; more testing would not change that the threshold misses most losses.

tips: Eliminate: A overlooks the threshold that misses most losses, and C reverses the finding, since the logs show the review runs as designed.
Final two: B beats D because design is judged first; an operating test of a control aimed at the wrong refunds cannot earn it credit.
Exam cue: check design before operation; a control that runs perfectly against the wrong cause earns little credit in residual risk.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Inherent and residual risk. Request for zero residual risk
questions.question: After a car rental company tokenized the card numbers it stores, the payments manager asks the risk analyst to record the card-data theft scenario's residual risk as zero. What is the analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Rate the residual risk that the change still leaves
options.B: Record zero residual risk with the manager's sign-off
options.C: Close the scenario and keep its entry as history
options.D: Ask internal audit to confirm the risk is eliminated

questions.key_concept: Residual risk is never zero; after a strong response the practitioner rates what remains rather than recording or closing it as gone.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the manager is asking the analyst to record.
questions.correct_explanation: Tokenization cuts the exposure of stored card numbers, but some risk remains, such as card data captured at the point of entry or misuse of the token system. Residual risk is never zero, so the analyst rates what is left on the usual scales for the owner to weigh against appetite. Asking internal audit is the runner-up: assurance may follow, but no review can confirm a zero that does not exist.

wrong_explanations.B: A sign-off cannot make residual risk zero; recording it would hide the exposure that remains from the owner and the risk profile.
wrong_explanations.C: Closing the scenario treats the risk as gone; it remains live at a lower level and still needs rating and monitoring.
wrong_explanations.D: Audit gives independent assurance later; it cannot confirm that a risk has been removed when some residual risk always remains.

tips: Eliminate: B and C both treat the risk as gone, one by recording zero and one by closing the scenario; residual risk is never zero.
Final two: A beats D because the analyst's job is to rate what remains; independent assurance cannot confirm a zero that cannot exist.
Exam cue: after any response, expect some residual risk; rate it and compare it with appetite rather than closing the risk.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Inherent and residual risk. Two scales in one unit
questions.question: A mining company's unit rates inherent risk on the enterprise scale, on which the board sets accepted risk levels, but residual risk on a vendor tool's 0–100 scores. What is the risk analyst's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The enterprise scale is less precise than the tool's scores
options.B: The tool's 0–100 scores are hard to show on a heat map
options.C: The inherent-to-residual gap no longer shows control effect
options.D: Residual ratings cannot be compared directly with risk appetite

questions.key_concept: Inherent and residual risk use the enterprise's common scale, so residual risk can be compared with appetite and the controls' effect seen.
questions.pre_read: Notice which of the unit's ratings left the enterprise scale.
questions.correct_explanation: The board states its appetite on the enterprise scale, so residual scores on a vendor's private 0–100 scale cannot be compared directly with it: nobody can show whether the unit's risks are within appetite, and owners cannot decide whether to accept or treat them. The lost inherent-to-residual gap is the runner-up: it hides how much the controls reduce risk, but the decision that rests on residual risk is the comparison with appetite.

wrong_explanations.A: Finer-grained scores are not more correct; the enterprise scale, with defined levels, is the common term every unit's ratings must use.
wrong_explanations.B: Any scale can be binned onto a heat map; display is a minor issue beside the decisions the ratings must support.
wrong_explanations.C: The lost gap hides how much the controls reduce risk, but the owner's accept-or-treat decision rests on comparing residual risk directly with appetite.

tips: Eliminate: A treats finer vendor scores as better than defined enterprise levels, and B is a display issue, since any scale can be binned onto a map.
Final two: D beats C because the accept-or-treat decision rests on residual risk against appetite; the lost gap matters less than that lost comparison.
Exam cue: inherent and residual risk must use the enterprise's common scale; otherwise residual risk cannot be compared with appetite.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286C Rev. 1 Section 2.2 (Normalization of Cybersecurity Risk Registers: the same rating criteria enable comparison and tracking); NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.2 (Assessment Approaches: semi-quantitative bins and scales have meaning only within the assessment); NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1 Section 2.1 (Overview of ERM: risk appetite and risk tolerance)
