questions.subtopic: 2A1 Risk events. Outage logs kept by two teams
questions.question: A food bank's IT help desk and warehouse team each log inventory-system outages; the two logs overlap, and each holds outages the other missed. What should the risk analyst do FIRST to rate likelihood?

options.A: Rate likelihood from the warehouse owner's outage estimate
options.B: Combine the logs, counting each shared outage once
options.C: Use sector outage rates for similar inventory systems
options.D: Have the IT owner run a single outage log from now on

questions.key_concept: Event data is made complete and counted once before it sets a likelihood; an enterprise's own cleaned records come before outside rates.
questions.pre_read: Look at the state of the data the analyst already holds before deciding where likelihood should come from.
questions.correct_explanation: Each log misses outages the other caught, and some outages appear in both, so neither log alone nor both added together give a true count. Merging the records so each outage counts once gives the food bank's own complete history, the best basis for likelihood. Sector outage rates are the runner-up: outside figures help when local history is short or missing, but here the records exist and need only cleaning.

wrong_explanations.A: An owner's estimate is judgment; with two logs of actual outages on hand, records give a firmer basis, and the estimate can later test the merged count.
wrong_explanations.C: Sector rates help when local history is thin, but they reflect other organizations' systems; the food bank's own records exist and need only matching.
wrong_explanations.D: A single log will improve future data, but it does nothing for the past outages the rating needs now; merging the existing records comes first.

tips: Eliminate: A swaps two logs of recorded outages for one person's estimate, and D fixes future logging but leaves the past outages the rating needs unmatched.
Final two: B beats C because the food bank's own records, once cleaned, show this system's history; outside rates are for when local history is missing or too short.
Exam cue: before event data sets a likelihood, make it complete and count each event once; clean your own records before reaching for outside figures.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Business impact analysis (BIA). Data that sets the recovery point
questions.question: A farm cooperative's grain-intake system holds truck weights, also printed on drivers' tickets, and price-setting protein results from samples discarded after testing. Which data should MOST shape the recovery point objective the risk analyst recommends?

options.A: Protein results recorded for each delivered load
options.B: Truck weights that the payments owner uses to pay members
options.C: Member bank details held for the payment runs
options.D: Intake summary reports built from the other records

questions.key_concept: The RPO follows the data the business can least afford to lose; records that can be entered again from another source tolerate a longer gap.
questions.pre_read: For each kind of data, ask what would happen to the records written since the last backup.
questions.correct_explanation: An RPO is set by how much data loss the business can tolerate. Protein results set each load's price, and any written since the last backup would be gone for good, because their samples were discarded, so they need the most recent restore point and set the RPO. Truck weights are the runner-up: they drive member payments, but any weights lost from the system can be keyed in again from the drivers' printed tickets.

wrong_explanations.B: Weights matter for member payments, but lost entries can be keyed in again from the drivers' printed tickets, so they tolerate more data loss than the protein results.
wrong_explanations.C: Bank details change little between backups, so a restore loses almost none; their sensitivity calls for confidentiality controls, not the most recent restore point.
wrong_explanations.D: Summary reports are built from the underlying records, so they can be produced again after a restore; they do not set how recent the restore point must be.

tips: Eliminate: C changes little between backups, so a restore loses almost nothing, and D can be rebuilt from the records beneath it; neither sets how recent the restore point must be.
Final two: A beats B because weights lost from the system can be keyed in again from the printed tickets, while protein results are lost with the discarded samples.
Exam cue: the RPO is set by the data the business can least afford to lose; ask whether lost records could be entered again from another source.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Risk register. Risk with a cause beyond control
questions.question: A wind farm operator's IT manager has kept lightning damage to turbine-control links out of the risk register, saying no one can control the weather. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Note lightning as an assumption behind the other ratings
options.B: Ask the operations owner to insure the links before rating
options.C: Have lightning damage entered and rated like other risks
options.D: Keep the register to risks whose causes the firm controls

questions.key_concept: A risk whose cause the enterprise cannot control still belongs in the register, because its impact can be reduced, shared or planned for.
questions.pre_read: Before agreeing to leave a risk out, ask what the register is for and who relies on it.
questions.correct_explanation: The register records risks by their effect on objectives, not by whether the cause can be prevented. Lightning cannot be stopped, but surge protection, backup links, spares and insurance can cut its impact, and the owner can weigh them only once the risk is rated. Noting lightning as an assumption is the runner-up: it keeps the hazard in view, but an assumption gets no rating, owner or response.

wrong_explanations.A: An assumption is noted, not rated, so lightning damage would get no likelihood, impact, owner or response, however large its harm.
wrong_explanations.B: Insurance is one possible response, but choosing it before the risk is rated skips the analysis that shows whether insurance, protection or acceptance fits.
wrong_explanations.D: Weather is an environmental threat source; risks are kept by their effect on objectives, and a register limited to controllable causes hides real exposure.

tips: Eliminate: D leaves out environmental threat sources, which belong in the register like any other, and B picks a response before the risk has been rated.
Final two: C beats A because a rated register entry gets an owner and a response, while an assumption keeps lightning in view without either.
Exam cue: a cause beyond the enterprise's control is no reason to leave a risk out; its impact can still be reduced, transferred or planned for.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Inherent and residual risk. Credit for a review that found nothing
questions.question: A copper mine's risk owner wants the assay-fraud scenario's residual rating lowered, as the lab's audit-trail review has found no altered results in three years. What is the risk analyst's GREATEST concern?

options.A: No new control has been added to justify a lower rating
options.B: Three clean years of review are too short to rely on
options.C: The control owner, not the risk owner, should request it
options.D: A broken review would show the same clean record

questions.key_concept: A detective control's clean record earns credit only once a test shows it would catch the event; a broken one also reports nothing.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each piece of evidence can and cannot show about how well the control works.
questions.correct_explanation: The review is a detective control, and three years without findings fits two stories: no one altered results, or the review cannot catch them. Silence alone cannot tell these apart, so it earns no extra credit until a test, such as seeding known altered test records, shows the review finds them. The short record is the runner-up: a longer clean run would carry the same doubt, since the gap is in what the evidence shows.

wrong_explanations.A: A rating can fall without a new control when evidence shows an existing one works, as restore-tested backups do; the doubt here is the evidence itself.
wrong_explanations.B: More clean years would not help: a review that cannot catch altered results stays silent for any length of time, so the record's length is not the issue.
wrong_explanations.C: A risk owner may ask for a re-rating and bring evidence; who asks matters less than whether the evidence shows the review works.

tips: Eliminate: A ties a lower rating to a new control, though tested existing controls also earn credit, and C fixes on who asked rather than on what the evidence shows.
Final two: D beats B because a broken detective control stays silent however long you wait; only a test that it catches altered results can earn the credit.
Exam cue: for a detective control, 'nothing found' proves little; ask for a test showing it would catch the event before giving it credit.

questions.question: IT closed a container shipping line's six-hour booking-system outage as low impact because no data was lost. Which is the BEST source for the risk analyst's record of the event's impact?

options.A: The booking owner's tally of missed sailings and penalties
options.B: The impact assessment in IT's incident report
options.C: An estimate based on the outage length and average bookings
options.D: Booking-outage losses reported by other shipping lines

questions.key_concept: An event's business loss comes from the owner of the process it hit; IT's incident record shows the technical side, such as data lost.
questions.pre_read: Ask who would actually see each kind of loss the outage caused.
questions.correct_explanation: A loss event is recorded with its full business impact, and IT sees only the technical side: no data lost. The booking owner can count the actual harm, such as containers that missed their sailing and penalties paid to customers. An estimate from outage length and average bookings is the runner-up: it is a fair fallback when no record exists, but it cannot show what this outage actually cost.

wrong_explanations.B: IT's report measures technical impact, such as data lost and time to restore; it does not see missed sailings or customer penalties, which fall on the business.
wrong_explanations.C: An average-based estimate is a fallback when actual figures are missing; it smooths over this outage's timing, such as whether a sailing closed during it.
wrong_explanations.D: Peer losses help rate a scenario when local history is thin, but this event happened at the line itself, and its own losses can be counted directly.

tips: Eliminate: B records only the technical side, such as data lost, and D draws on other lines' events when this one happened at the line and can be counted directly.
Final two: A beats C because the owner can count what this outage actually cost; an average-based estimate misses its timing and is for when no record exists.
Exam cue: an event's impact is the business loss it caused; get it from the owner of the affected process, not from IT's restore record or an average.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Threat modeling and threat landscape. Sharing a model trained on patient reports
questions.question: A generic drug maker plans to give university researchers a copy of its model trained on patients' adverse-reaction reports. Which AI-specific threat in this plan should MOST concern the risk analyst?

options.A: Model extraction by researchers sending repeated queries
options.B: Membership inference revealing whose reports trained the model
options.C: Data poisoning through false adverse-reaction reports
options.D: Evasion inputs crafted to make the copy misjudge cases

questions.key_concept: Sharing a model trained on personal data lets its holders test whether a person's record was in the training set, exposing private facts.
questions.pre_read: Work out what holders of a copy could do that outsiders could not do before.
questions.correct_explanation: With a copy in hand, the researchers, or anyone the copy reaches, can run membership inference: testing whether a person's report was in the training data, which reveals that the person had a drug reaction. The plan creates this exposure, and patients bear the harm. Data poisoning through false reports is the runner-up: it is a real AI threat, but it targets training data whether or not the model is shared.

wrong_explanations.A: Extraction rebuilds a model from its answers to many queries; the researchers are being given the model itself, so this plan leaves nothing to extract.
wrong_explanations.C: False reports could skew future training, but that threat exists with or without sharing; the plan's new exposure is to patients' privacy through the copy.
wrong_explanations.D: Evasion makes a model misjudge crafted inputs, which would mislead only whoever relies on the researchers' copy; it exposes no patient data.

tips: Eliminate: A attacks a model the researchers will already hold, and D misleads only users of the copy's outputs; neither touches the patients behind the training data.
Final two: B beats C because sharing a copy opens a new privacy attack on the patients, while poisoning through false reports exists whether or not the model is shared.
Exam cue: when a change gives others a model, ask what that access newly allows; a model trained on personal data can reveal who was in it.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Vulnerability management. AI camera that spots batteries in scrap
questions.question: A steel recycler's AI camera flags lithium batteries in incoming scrap for removal before shredding; under 1% of loads contain one. Which evidence BEST shows the risk analyst how well the camera works?

options.A: The shredding process owner's self-assessment of the camera
options.B: Number of batteries it has flagged on the live sorting line
options.C: Number of misses per 100 known batteries in test loads
options.D: Its overall accuracy rate on a labeled set of test loads

questions.key_concept: A rare-item detector can score high overall accuracy while missing most targets; its misses among known targets show how well it works.
questions.pre_read: Think about what each figure counts, and what it leaves out.
questions.correct_explanation: With batteries in under 1% of loads, a camera that flagged nothing would still score over 99% accuracy, so the headline figure hides the failure that matters: a missed battery reaching the shredder. Its miss rate, the share of known test batteries it missed, measures exactly that. Overall accuracy is the runner-up: it comes from the same kind of labeled test, but it mixes the rare batteries with a great many easy empty loads.

wrong_explanations.A: A self-assessment records the owner's view, not test results; it shows confidence in the camera rather than how many batteries it would miss.
wrong_explanations.B: Batteries flagged in live use show the camera is active, but without knowing how many passed unflagged, the count says nothing about misses.
wrong_explanations.D: Accuracy counts every correct call, and almost every load has no battery, so a camera that misses most batteries can still score near 100%.

tips: Eliminate: B counts batteries caught in live use with no record of those that slipped past, and A is the owner's view rather than a test result.
Final two: C beats D because accuracy is swamped by the many empty loads, while the miss rate measures the failure the camera exists to prevent.
Exam cue: when a control hunts for something rare, judge it by what it misses among known cases, not by its overall hit rate.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Risk scenario development and evaluation. Altered paint formulas
questions.question: A paint manufacturer's draft scenario of an insider altering paint formulas in its batch-control system rates impact as the cost of one spoiled batch. What is the risk analyst's BEST next step?

options.A: Rate impact on the time needed to restore altered formulas from backup
options.B: Ask the production owner how long altered batches could go unnoticed
options.C: Rate likelihood on how many staff can edit batch formulas
options.D: Add the insider's most likely motive to the scenario

questions.key_concept: When data is altered rather than lost, harm keeps growing until someone notices, so time to detection drives the scenario's impact.
questions.pre_read: Ask what drives the cost of this kind of event before choosing a step.
questions.correct_explanation: Altered formulas do not stop production: every batch made with them is faulty, and the harm grows with each batch shipped until someone notices. The production owner knows batch volumes and where quality checks would, or would not, catch the change. Restore time is the runner-up: it sizes an outage, but altered formulas leave the system running, and restoring them only ends harm already done.

wrong_explanations.A: Restore time sizes an outage, but altered formulas leave production running; the cost lies in faulty batches made before anyone notices, not in the restore.
wrong_explanations.C: Edit rights bear on how likely the change is, not on how much harm it does; the draft's gap is in its impact figure.
wrong_explanations.D: A motive helps judge the threat source and likelihood, but it does not change how many faulty batches ship before anyone notices.

tips: Eliminate: C and D both refine likelihood, through edit rights and motive, while the draft's weakness is its impact figure.
Final two: B beats A because altered data does harm while the system keeps running; time to detection, not restore time, sets the cost.
Exam cue: for tampering or silent errors, ask how long they could run unnoticed; that period usually drives the impact.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Risk assessment concepts and standards. Controllers moved to a hotter site
questions.question: A textile mill's loom controllers, with two faults in eight years, were moved last month beside new dryers and now run 15°C hotter. Which is the BEST basis for the risk analyst's fault-likelihood rating?

options.A: Threat reports on attacks against textile control systems
options.B: The mill's own eight-year fault record for the controllers
options.C: The line owner's estimate of the controllers' remaining life
options.D: The maker's failure-rate data at the new operating temperature

questions.key_concept: Own history predicts equipment failure best while conditions hold; after a change such as more heat, prefer data for the new conditions.
questions.pre_read: Ask under what conditions each source's figures were gathered.
questions.correct_explanation: A controller fault is a non-adversarial event, rated from historical and empirical data, and running hotter changes how often electronics fail. The maker's failure-rate data at the new temperature describes the controllers as they now run. The mill's own eight-year record is the runner-up: own history is usually the best source, but it was gathered in cooler conditions that no longer apply.

wrong_explanations.A: Threat reports describe attackers, but a controller fault is a non-adversarial event; its likelihood comes from failure data, not intent or capability.
wrong_explanations.B: Own history is normally the best basis, but these eight years were spent in cooler conditions, so they may understate faults at the new, hotter site.
wrong_explanations.C: An estimate of remaining life is one person's judgment, a fallback when data is missing; measured failure rates are stronger evidence.

tips: Eliminate: A treats an equipment fault as an attack, and C relies on one person's judgment where measured failure data exists.
Final two: D beats B because the eight-year record was gathered in cooler conditions; the maker's data matches how the controllers now run.
Exam cue: past records predict best while conditions hold; after a move, an upgrade or a new load, look for data that fits the new conditions.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Business impact analysis (BIA). Timing for a new portal
questions.question: A crop insurer has approved an online policy portal for farmers, due to go live next year. When is it BEST for the risk analyst to have the portal's BIA carried out?

options.A: Before the portal owner settles its hosting and recovery design
options.B: After go-live, once the portal owner has real usage figures
options.C: When IT and the hosting vendor agree on the portal's recovery time
options.D: During user acceptance testing of the finished portal

questions.key_concept: A new system's BIA is done at its start, so recovery needs shape the design rather than being retrofitted later.
questions.pre_read: Ask which decisions the BIA's results feed, and when those decisions are made.
questions.correct_explanation: A BIA shows how long the business can manage without the portal and how much data loss it can bear, and the recovery objectives drawn from it drive the hosting and recovery design. Done before that design is settled, it shapes the build; done later, gaps mean costly retrofits. Waiting for real usage figures is the runner-up: they can refine the BIA after go-live, but the design would already be fixed.

wrong_explanations.B: Real figures can refine the BIA later, but by go-live the hosting and recovery design is fixed, and changing it then costs far more.
wrong_explanations.C: A recovery time agreed by IT and a vendor should come from the BIA's results; setting it first lets capability, not business need, decide.
wrong_explanations.D: By acceptance testing the portal is built; recovery needs found then mean redesign or a gap the business must live with.

tips: Eliminate: C lets IT and the vendor fix a recovery time the BIA should inform, and D comes after the portal is already built.
Final two: A beats B because the BIA's results should shape the recovery design; real figures can refine it later but cannot cheaply reopen a fixed design.
Exam cue: for a new system, the BIA comes at the start and is revisited as the design changes; recovery needs are designed in, not added later.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Risk register. Showing supplier risks together
questions.question: An e-scooter rental operator's board wants its supplier-related risks shown together, but each of the 140 register entries records only a scenario, owner and ratings. Which change should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: A list of supplier entries compiled by each risk owner
options.B: A keyword search of scenarios that name a supplier
options.C: A risk category on each entry, chosen from one agreed list
options.D: A separate register for supplier risks with procurement as owner

questions.key_concept: A risk category on every register entry, drawn from one agreed list, lets entries be grouped, compared and combined, such as all supplier risks.
questions.pre_read: Weigh how each option would find every relevant entry, and keep finding them.
questions.correct_explanation: A category field drawn from one agreed list lets the register be filtered and combined by theme, so supplier risks can be shown together now and each time the profile is reported, and the same entries can roll up to the enterprise view. A keyword search is the runner-up: it is quick, but it misses scenarios that do not name a supplier and depends on who picks the search words.

wrong_explanations.A: Owners' lists answer this request once, in each owner's own terms; nothing in the register then lets the next request be met the same way.
wrong_explanations.B: A search finds only scenarios that happen to name a supplier and depends on who picks the words, so results are incomplete and hard to repeat.
wrong_explanations.D: A separate register splits the risk profile, so supplier risks can no longer be compared or combined with the rest; one register with categories avoids that.

tips: Eliminate: A is a one-off list in each owner's own terms, and D splits supplier risks from the rest of the profile, so they cannot be combined.
Final two: C beats B because an agreed category finds every supplier entry the same way each time; a keyword search misses entries that name no supplier.
Exam cue: to group, compare or roll up register entries, look for a common field, such as a category, drawn from one agreed list.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Risk analysis methodologies. Impact ratings that scatter
questions.question: A veterinary practice group's impact scale gives five levels only as names, minor to severe; rating one group-wide records outage, its 12 clinic managers used all five. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Average the 12 managers' ratings into one level for the group
options.B: Define each level with examples of cost, downtime and harm
options.C: Have the outage scenario's risk owner choose the group's rating
options.D: Switch to a finer 1-to-10 scale for impact ratings

questions.key_concept: Rating levels need definitions with examples, such as dollar and downtime ranges; without them, raters use private meanings and one risk gets any rating.
questions.pre_read: Ask why people rating the same event would land so far apart.
questions.correct_explanation: When a scale gives only names, each manager reads 'moderate' or 'severe' through their own clinic's experience, so the same outage gets every rating. Defining each level with examples, such as dollar ranges, hours of downtime and harm to animals in care, fixes the cause for this and every later rating. Having the risk owner choose is the runner-up: it settles this one scenario but leaves the scale undefined.

wrong_explanations.A: Averaging ordinal levels gives a middle figure no manager chose and hides the spread; the managers still mean different things by each level.
wrong_explanations.C: The owner's choice settles this one rating, but the scale stays undefined, so the next scenario will scatter the same way across the group.
wrong_explanations.D: More steps on an undefined scale give more room to disagree and a false look of precision; the levels still lack a shared meaning.

tips: Eliminate: A averages ordinal levels, which carry order but not size, and D adds finer steps to a scale whose levels still lack meaning.
Final two: B beats C because defining the levels fixes why ratings scatter; an owner's pick settles one scenario and leaves the cause in place.
Exam cue: when raters disagree widely on the same risk, look first at the scale's definitions before averaging, re-scaling or overruling them.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Inherent and residual risk. New records in a tested store
questions.question: A contract research lab's residual breach rating for its sample database assumed coded animal data; it now also holds named patients' trial records under the same tested controls. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Raise the inherent rating and keep the residual rating
options.B: Require the control owner to restrict database access further
options.C: Re-rate the residual risk to reflect the higher impact
options.D: Compare the inherent rating with appetite for the risk owner

questions.key_concept: Residual risk is what controls leave of the exposure, so data that is more harmful to lose raises it even with unchanged controls.
questions.pre_read: Ask which part of the risk changed, and which ratings that change reaches.
questions.correct_explanation: Residual risk is what remains of the exposure once controls work, so it moves when the exposure moves, not only when controls change. Named patients' records make a breach far more harmful than coded animal data, so the same tested controls now leave more residual risk, which needs re-rating before anyone compares it with appetite. Raising only the inherent rating is the runner-up: it wrongly assumes unchanged controls absorb the whole increase.

wrong_explanations.A: Inherent risk does rise, but the same controls cannot absorb the extra harm a breach of named records would cause, so an unchanged residual rating understates today's exposure.
wrong_explanations.B: Tightening access before the new exposure is rated is treatment before analysis; the analyst re-rates the change and the risk owner decides on any added control.
wrong_explanations.D: Treatment decisions compare residual risk with appetite; inherent risk credits no control, so comparing it with appetite would overstate the need for more treatment.

tips: Eliminate: B picks a control before the change is rated, and D compares inherent risk with appetite, where residual risk belongs.
Final two: C beats A because residual risk depends on the exposure the controls protect as well as on the controls; when that exposure grows, residual risk grows too.
Exam cue: a change in what an asset holds or supports can move residual risk even when the controls stay the same; re-rate both levels.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (residual risk); NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 3.4 Task 4-2 (Update Risk Assessment: updates assess how selected risk factors have changed, such as newly affected assets, likelihoods and impacts)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2B5.2 (Control Effectiveness and the Residual Gap: residual risk is re-rated when the data a control protects changes, such as newly added sensitive records), 2B5.1 (Inherent, Current and Residual Risk) and 2B5.3 (residual risk is reviewed again when the business changes). questions.subtopic: 2A2 Threat modeling and threat landscape. Tuned open-weight model
questions.question: A geological survey tuned a hub-downloaded open-weight model on its own slope photos to flag landslides; its data team says tuning removed any threat from the model's origin. Which is the risk analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Add prompt injection as the landslide scenario's main threat
options.B: Retest the tuned model's accuracy on new slope photos
options.C: Treat the hub's download count as evidence of safety
options.D: Keep the tampered-model threat in the landslide scenario

questions.key_concept: A backdoor planted in a downloaded model can survive fine-tuning and pass ordinary accuracy tests, so the supply-chain threat stays in the scenario.
questions.pre_read: Ask what tuning changes in a model, and what it leaves alone.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST's adversarial machine learning taxonomy notes that backdoors planted in pre-trained models can persist after downstream users fine-tune them, so tuning on the survey's photos does not remove a threat that came with the download. The tampered-model threat stays in the landslide scenario for rating. Retesting accuracy is the runner-up: a backdoor fires only on inputs carrying its trigger, so ordinary slope photos would still score well.

wrong_explanations.A: Prompt injection targets models that follow instructions found in their input; a model that classifies slope photos follows none, while its downloaded weights are the exposed asset.
wrong_explanations.B: A backdoor changes outputs only for inputs carrying its trigger, so a tuned model can score well on ordinary photos while the planted behavior remains.
wrong_explanations.C: Download counts show popularity, not provenance; a widely used model can still carry a planted backdoor, and NIST advises treating such models as untrusted components.

tips: Eliminate: C treats popularity as proof of a clean model, and A names an instruction attack against a model that only classifies photos.
Final two: D beats B because tuning does not strip a planted backdoor, and an accuracy retest on ordinary photos cannot show a trigger that is absent from them.
Exam cue: when a team says retraining or tuning removed a supply-chain threat, keep the threat rated until evidence about the model's origin addresses it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Section 3.2.2 (Model Poisoning Attacks: maliciously designed pre-trained models can carry backdoors that persist after downstream fine-tuning); NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Section 2.3 (Poisoning Attacks and Mitigations: targeted and backdoor poisoning affect a small set of target samples); NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Section 3.2.3 (Mitigations: risks can be reduced by understanding models as untrusted system components)

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Risk scenario development and evaluation. Choosing a tabletop scenario
questions.question: An irrigation district's first tabletop exercise will test how its managers escalate and decide during a serious disruption. Which scenario should the risk practitioner propose as BEST?

options.A: A peak-season pump outage its risk owners rank highest
options.B: A dam collapse that the district's engineers rate implausible
options.C: A routine canal leak of the kind field crews repair
options.D: A cyberattack scenario that names no asset, owner or time

questions.key_concept: A tabletop scenario should be severe but plausible, drawn from the risks owners rank highest, so the decisions it tests are ones they may face.
questions.pre_read: Read what the exercise is meant to test, then weigh each scenario against it.
questions.correct_explanation: A tabletop exercise tests decisions, so its scenario should press managers to escalate and choose under conditions they could genuinely meet. A peak-season pump outage that risk owners rank highest is severe and plausible, and its lessons attach to a scenario they own. The dam collapse is the runner-up: worst cases can be exercised, but one the engineers rate implausible turns play into debate about whether it could happen.

wrong_explanations.B: Worst cases may be exercised, but one rated implausible draws debate about the scenario itself, and a first exercise gains more from risks owners rank highest.
wrong_explanations.C: Field crews handle routine leaks without managers, so the scenario would not call for the escalation and decisions the exercise is meant to test.
wrong_explanations.D: A scenario with no asset, owner or timing gives participants nothing concrete to decide on, so their choices cannot be tested or rated afterward.

tips: Eliminate: C is handled by field crews without escalation, and D is a generic scenario too vague for anyone to make concrete decisions.
Final two: A beats B because a severe but plausible scenario tests decisions owners may face; one rated implausible invites argument about the scenario instead of the response.
Exam cue: pick exercise scenarios from the register's top risks: serious enough to test escalation, credible enough that the lessons change real plans.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.5.3 (Exercises: tabletop exercises are discussion-based and examine roles, responsibilities, coordination and decision making); NIST SP 800-84 Section 4.3 (Develop the Tabletop Exercise Material: the scenario is a narrative of a hypothetical incident meant to inspire responses that demonstrate the exercise objectives)

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Business impact analysis (BIA). A newer scanner model
questions.question: A patent office revises its BIA when a process, dependency, obligation or outage limit changes; a change review found newer same-supplier scanners change none of these. Which is the risk analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Revise the BIA now with the filing process owner's input
options.B: Add the newer scanners' failure likelihood to the BIA
options.C: Set the scanning RTO from the newer model's repair time
options.D: Have the swap logged for the next scheduled BIA update

questions.key_concept: A BIA is revised when its triggers are met; a change that meets none, such as like-for-like equipment, waits for the next scheduled update.
questions.pre_read: Check the change against each trigger the stem lists before choosing how much work it needs.
questions.correct_explanation: The office's BIA names the changes that call for a revision, and its change review found the newer scanners meet none of them: processes, dependencies, obligations and outage limits stay as rated. Logging the swap for the next scheduled update keeps the record complete without rework. Revising now with the filing owner is the runner-up: it spends owners' time re-confirming impact that the review already found unchanged.

wrong_explanations.A: The BIA's own triggers decide when it is revised, and the change review found none met, so revising now repeats work without changing any impact or priority.
wrong_explanations.B: A BIA assumes the disruption happens and leaves likelihood out; how often the newer scanners might fail belongs in the risk assessment.
wrong_explanations.C: Recovery objectives come from the business through the BIA, not from what equipment can deliver, and nothing here changed the outage the process can bear.

tips: Eliminate: B puts likelihood into a BIA, which assumes the disruption happens, and C sets a recovery objective from equipment capability instead of business impact.
Final two: D beats A because the BIA's revision triggers, all unmet here, decide its timing; revising now spends owners' time on impact the review found unchanged.
Exam cue: when the stem says no revision or review trigger is met, the scheduled cycle is the proportionate answer; a met trigger calls for revising now.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.6 (Plan Maintenance: when a significant change occurs, the BIA is updated to identify new contingency requirements or priorities); NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.6 (Plan Maintenance: the plan is reviewed for accuracy and completeness at an organization-defined frequency or whenever significant changes occur)

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Risk events. CVs sent without consent
questions.question: A recruitment firm records each CV it sends and each candidate's consent in its CRM. Which source would BEST show the risk analyst how often consultants send CVs without consent?

options.A: Complaint records in the CRM about CVs sent without consent
options.B: CRM records of CVs sent without any matching consent entry
options.C: Regulator notices fining other recruiters for the practice
options.D: The placements process owner's estimate of its frequency

questions.key_concept: Complaints capture only events people notice and report; a complete record of every transaction shows far more reliably how often an event occurs.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each source would miss.
questions.correct_explanation: Every CV sent and every consent is recorded in the CRM, so matching the two finds each unconsented submission, whether or not anyone noticed it. That complete count is the firm's own event record for the scenario. Complaints are the runner-up: they are a real internal source, but they count only the cases a candidate noticed and chose to report, so they understate how often it happens.

wrong_explanations.A: Complaints are a real internal source, but they count only the submissions a candidate learned of and chose to report, so they understate how often it happens.
wrong_explanations.C: Enforcement against other recruiters shows the consequence and that the practice exists in the sector, not how often this firm's consultants do it.
wrong_explanations.D: An owner's estimate is judgment, useful when records are missing; here the CRM holds every submission and consent, which is stronger evidence.

tips: Eliminate: C describes other firms' penalties rather than this firm's frequency, and D offers one person's judgment where complete records exist.
Final two: B beats A because matching every submission to its consent finds each event, while complaints catch only those a candidate noticed and reported.
Exam cue: for how often an event occurs, prefer a complete internal record of every transaction over sources that depend on someone noticing and speaking up.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 3.1 Task 1-4 (Identify Information Sources: information sources can be internal or external to the organization); NIST IR 8286A Rev. 1 Section 2.3.2.1 (Improving Estimation Based on Knowledge of Prior Events: practitioners can review a system's actual records of past events to inform likelihood estimates)
